.SHORT TERM...
(Today through Sunday)
Issued at 209 AM EST Sat Nov 7 2026

Cooler air continues to spread into north and central Georgia with 
northwesterly flow in the wake of the cold front. Low temperatures 
this morning are expected to be in the upper 30s to mid 40s in areas 
north of I-85 and in the upper 40s to near 50 in areas to the south. 
As surface high pressure approaches the Southeast, a tight pressure 
gradient will lead to breezy NW winds in portions of north and west 
Georgia, which could be between 10-15 mph with gusts up to 25 mph. 
High temperatures today are forecast to be in the 60s to low 70s in 
north Georgia and low to mid 70s in central Georgia. Low 
temperatures tonight into Sunday morning are expected to be in the 
mid to upper 30s in areas along and north of I-85, with some low 30s 
possible in the highest elevations along with patches of frost. A
Frost Advisory will likely be needed in portions of north and 
west Georgia. In areas south of I-85, lows on Sunday morning are 
forecast to be in the 40s. Highs on Sunday will be similar to 
today, in the 60s to mid 70s areawide. The influence of the 
aforementioned high pressure will inhibit rain chances through the
weekend.

&&

.LONG TERM...
(Sunday night through Friday)
Issued at 209 AM EST Sat Nov 7 2026

By Monday afternoon and evening a low pressure system will have 
pushed into the northeast with our area under a more zonal flow 
with an area of low pressure over Mexico into the SW and Texas. 
This pattern will generally be what we are under through Tuesday. 
Beginning on Tuesday the low pressure system begins to track east 
into the Arklatex but at this time moisture looks on track to stay
south of the area and stick to the Gulf. This will result in rain
chances less than 10% through mid next week. Temperatures will 
decrease into the 30s overnight beginning as early as Saturday 
morning and lasting through at least Tuesday morning. This will 
likely warrant frost/freeze products as the growing season 
continues in north Georgia. High temps will also lower into the 
mid to upper 60s this weekend. Rain chances may return late next 
week into next weekend with broad troughing over much of the 
eastern CONUS potentially bringing in moisture from the west as an
area of low pressure pushes into the gulf. Looking to the long 
term, the CPC has placed our area in a slight risk for below 
normal temperatures. We are looking at the potential for a deep 
trough over the southeast bringing in cooler air from Canada. This
will be yet another shot of cold air likely although it's a bit 
too soon to talk about how low the temps will get.

Area Forecast Discussion
National Weather Service Austin/San Antonio TX
537 AM CST Sat Nov 7 2026

...New AVIATION...

.KEY MESSAGES...
Updated at 533 AM CST Sat Nov 7 2026

- Wet, cloudy, and cool this weekend into Monday with steady rain 
  developing by tonight.

- Beneficial rains across the region with manageable rainfall
  rates.

- Isolated flooding possible where any locally heavier rain
  aligns.

- Dries out and trends milder mid to late week.

&&

.SHORT TERM...
(Today through Sunday)
Issued at 1223 AM CST Sat Nov 7 2026

As has been previously mentioned, a shortwave is forecast to 
eventually amplify and move southward as a nearly cut-off low while 
it approaches Texas. As it does so it will redirect moisture over 
our area as mid-level winds shift southwesterly. This will also 
result in the development of a lee-side trough over the eastern 
flanks of the Mexican plateau, which in turn increases the supply of 
low-level moisture streaming from the Gulf. The combination of these 
two moisture streams overriding atop cool air (isentropic lift) will 
support a rather broad rain event that may start as early as this 
morning along the Rio Grande and Edwards Plateau. We then expect 
rain chances to spread eastward across much of South-Central Texas 
throughout the day and into Saturday night. Because of the extensive 
cloud deck and rain cooled air highs today are expected to be 
somewhat cooler then the past few days. We are currently forecasting 
highs in the low to mid 60s for areas north and west of the I-35 
Corridor while areas south of this should see slightly warmer highs 
in the low to mid 70s as it will take longer to see rain over these 
areas. 

The rains become more widespread throughout the evening and into 
early Sunday morning. We anticipate rain intensity to remain mostly 
light to moderate with hourly rates, generally below an inch per 
hour as instability remains very limited across the area. There is 
however the possibility that some of the embedded cells could 
include thunderstorms, which would then enhance locally heavier rain 
rates, which could reach upwards to the 1 to 2 inch per hour range. 
It's these cells that we would need to concentrate on for any 
possible isolated flooding, especially if they enter our urban 
corridors or begin training over the same areas. As such, WPC 
continues to include much of the region along and west of the I-35 
corridor in a level 1 of 4 risk for flooding today through early 
Sunday morning. However, the vast majority of the rain, remains of 
the beneficial variety across our region. We also anticipate Sunday 
to be a very dreary, damp and downright miserable rainy day. This is 
also when we expect the bulk of the rain to fall across the entire 
forecast area.

&&

.LONG TERM...
(Sunday night through Friday)
Issued at 1223 AM CST Sat Nov 7 2026

By Sunday evening we could see a lull and decrease in rain across 
our northern and eastern areas including the Austin metro before we 
see another round of rain form over the Rio Grande and Southern 
Edwards Plateau areas. This 2nd round should continue pushing 
eastward late Sunday evening and continuing through the overnight 
hours into Monday morning. Latest global model ensembles now have 
this batch of rain sticking around through the day Monday and not 
clearing until Monday evening. As previously mentioned we could see 
some heavier embedded cells in this batch of rain that would be 
capable of producing heavier rainfall rates across locations that 
are already saturated with earlier rains during the event. WPC 
highlights a level 1 to 2 risk for flooding across the vast majority 
of our region from Sunday into Monday. As for amounts, we should see 
fairly widespread totals in the 1 to 3 inch range with some isolated 
pockets of up to 5 inches not out of the question for areas that see 
repeated rounds of rainfall. However, almost everyone should see at 
least a half inch to an inch when all is said and done. These totals 
may seem like a lot but we arent expecting any heavy torrential 
downpours but rather some good old fashioned steady cool rain that 
will occur over a period of several days rather than all at once.

As far as highs go, with the steady rainfall and extensive cloud 
cover we may see some areas struggle to break out of the mid 50s for 
highs with most remaining in the low to mid 60s producing yet 
another dreary and raw day for Monday across our forecast area. Lows 
however wont drop off too much as the clouds should keep most of the 
area fairly insulated and prevent any radiational cooling from 
happening with most staying in the upper 40s to near 50 degrees. 
Beyond Monday as we finally begin to dry out we should see highs 
rebound back near 70 for Tuesday with temps well into the 70s to 
round out the end of the week along with lows remaining in the
50s.

.DISCUSSION...
KEY MESSAGE 1...Widespread rain gradually ends this morning. Rain
will be heavy at times southeast MA and RI, where flood risk is
greatest. Another round of lighter showers this afternoon into
Sunday.

Broad low pressure along a stalled front across eastern MA and
RI will slowly move offshore this afternoon and evening. This 
low pressure should finally reach Downeast Maine and Nova Scotia
around daybreak Sunday.

While this means the widespread rainfall should be offshore by
this afternoon, we will still have to contend with a rather
potent mid level low. This low should pass overhead tonight. The
colder air aloft will result in increased lapse rates, which in
turn should generate some showers later today and tonight. 
These showers will be much lighter in intensity. The greatest 
coverage of showers should be towards northern MA. 

Above normal temperatures continue yet again today, but will be
trending closer to normal. Expecting only slightly above normal
temperatures for Sunday. 

KEY MESSAGE 2...Cooler and drier conditions arrive next week,
though it could turn unsettled once more towards the second 
half of the week.

Colder air aloft continues to shift into southern New England
for the start of next week as yet another upper level trough 
tracks into the region. This is a bit more notable at 850 mb and
500 mb, where temperatures fall to just below 0C and to around 
- 24C at those respective levels. With cooler air aloft and a 
passing shortwave just to our north, we could see some showers 
around Monday. 925 mb temperatures fall to around 2-4C by Monday
night, supporting lows falling further into the 30s and low 
40s, with highs Tuesday and the start of the week generally in 
the 50s to low 60s. Cooler nights will persist through the week.

NAEFS and other ensemble guidance indicate no significant
deviations from the climatological percentiles for temperatures 
or moisture for this coming week, though did note 90th
percentile zonal winds aloft Monday into Wednesday just to the
south of the region. Persistent westerly flow with notably
breezy conditions Monday and Tuesday is expected. Winds
generally stay westerly through much of the week, given the
series of fronts expected to move through the region. With the
drier conditions (PWATS to around 0.5" and less and dew points 
back in the 30s and 40s) at the surface, not much in the way of 
precipitation is expected with these frontal passages; just 
cooler air. Occasional cloudiness is expected at most with 
passing moist air aloft.

Towards the second half of next week, guidance has started to
pick up on the possible development of another low pressure
originating from just to the south of the region along/just off 
the mid- Atlantic coast. This looks to be driven by the approach
of an upper level shortwave tracking from Canada southeast into
the mid-Atlantic region. With this possible system, we could see 
the return of more unsettled conditions for the second half of 
the week.

.KEY MESSAGES...

- Dry conditions and a warming trend will occur this weekend 
  into early next week.

- The next chance for precipitation is forecast mid-late next 
  week and will likely be accompanied by cooler temperatures.

&&

.DISCUSSION...
Issued at 213 AM CST Sat Nov 7 2026

An upper low tied to the subtropical jet stream will slowly 
meander across northern Mexico and Texas over the weekend and 
into early next week, yielding expansive, persistent ridging 
across the central CONUS. The polar jet stream will remain 
active with a series of disturbances getting shuttled eastward 
and southeastward across southern Canada and the northern and
eastern Great Lakes during this time frame. However, the core 
of this jet will remain displaced far enough to our north to 
keep these disturbances and any associated precipitation a safe 
distance away from our forecast area. Thus, the net result of 
this weather pattern for northern Illinois and northwestern 
Indiana will be precipitation-free conditions and a warming 
trend from near-normal high temperatures today to above normal 
high temperatures (likely in the low-mid 60s) by Monday and 
Tuesday. Low temperatures will also generally trend upward from 
this morning's widespread freezing/near-freezing conditions, 
though additional near to slightly below freezing lows could be 
observed in some spots again Sunday morning and once more Monday
morning.

Clear nocturnal skies and light/calm winds may lead to some 
localized patchy fog development this morning in a few 
locations, but this isn't expected to become a widespread issue.
Interestingly, multiple pieces of forecast guidance are 
signaling that advection fog may drift into our area 
tonight/Sunday morning as modest low-level warm/moist advection 
in advance of a surface trough/weak cold front attempts to 
saturate the planetary boundary layer. An examination of HRRR, 
RAP, and RRFS forecast soundings suggests that there may be just
enough separation between surface temperatures and the steadily
rising surface dew points to have this influx of low-level 
moisture manifest itself as more of a low stratus deck, but at 
least localized visibility reductions at ground level do appear 
to be a distinct possibility tonight into Sunday morning -- 
particularly with northward and westward extent across northern 
Illinois.

Ensemble guidance remains in relatively good agreement on a 
pattern change occurring during the latter half of this upcoming
week as several upper-level disturbances amalgamate to yield 
deep aggregate longwave troughing across the northeastern 
quadrant of the CONUS. This troughing will likely end up 
encompassing most or all of the Great Lakes region, and there 
has been an increasing ensemble signal for lake effect 
precipitation occurring in our forecast area late next week as a
result. Individual shortwaves embedded within the longer 
wavelength troughing could also deliver a broader wave or two of
synoptic precipitation to the area during the mid-late week 
time frame as well, though there has been less spatiotemporal 
consistency and overall agreement amongst Grand Ensemble members
on this possibility being realized. As the composite longwave 
trough becomes established, a cooler air mass will also 
barge into the region and could end up influencing what types 
of precipitation are seen here late next week. Just how cold 
temperatures will get in our area late next week into next 
weekend will depend on the exact longitudinal positioning of the
longwave trough axis, which is an item of relatively low 
confidence at this time.

Ogorek

.WHAT HAS CHANGED...

.KEY MESSAGES...
- 1) Dry and seasonable this weekend.

- 2) Dry weather continues next week before a colder and more

&&

.DISCUSSION...
KEY MESSAGE 1...Dry and seasonable this weekend.

High pressure will build near and south of the region through
the weekend as an upper trough axis pulls away to the east.
Brisk west to northwest winds will usher in cooler, more
seasonable temperatures. Winds will gust up to 25 to 35 mph
today (up to around 40 mph at higher elevations). Sunday will
still be breezy, but about 5-10 mph lower than today.

Wave clouds/stratocu likely persist west of I-81 much of today
with a few sprinkles or flurries possible out that way. It will
be mainly clear and dry otherwise through the weekend.

The central Virginia piedmont will be closer to the high and
have a chance to decouple (winds going light/calm) tonight and
again Sunday night. If this happens, near freezing temperatures
would result. May consider frost/freeze headlines for Fauquier,
Culpeper, Stafford, Spotsylvania, Prince William, Orange,
Greene, Madison, Rappahannock, Nelson, and Albemarle Counties
from late this evening through Sunday morning.
 

KEY MESSAGE 2...Dry weather continues next week before a colder and more 
unsettled pattern ensues by Friday.

Amplified flow within the northern stream will allow for a series of 
dry cold frontal passages across the area next week. After the first 
boundary pushes through late in the weekend, an additional system 
races through on Tuesday. These are moisture starved air masses so 
the only notable changes will be an increase in wind speeds and the 
reinforcement of drier air. Through the middle of the week, skies 
should largely be clear which would support abundant sunshine. Daily 
high temperatures will mainly be in the 60s, with 50s across the 
mountains. One exception would be on Tuesday which is the mildest 
day of the period as highs return to the low 70s. Nighttime 
conditions will be seasonably chilly owing to the dry air and lack 
of cloud cover. Most nights should favor low temperatures in the mid 
30s to mid 40s, but with localized pockets of upper 20s to low 30s 
across sheltered mountain and river valleys. This may lead to some 
frost/freeze concerns where the growing season continues (most spots 
east of the Blue Ridge).

Toward the latter half of the next work week, global models continue 
to advertise a broad deepening trough approaching from the Upper 
Midwest. This eventually evolves into more of an omega block setup 
with building heights over the western states and troughing across 
the eastern Pacific. The global ensemble box-and-whisker plots show 
a decided drop in temperatures. Cold temperatures aloft underneath 
this upper low could even spread some rain or snow showers over the 
Alleghenies on Friday. Uncertainty remains high though, but a

Weak to moderate Santa Ana winds will peak this morning. A trough
digging into Baja California from the northeast will bring 
offshore surface pressure gradients and upper level wind support. 
All these components will peak this morning, and gusty winds are 
expected for the wind prone corridor of LA and Ventura Counties. A
Wind Advisory has been issued from 2 AM to 2 PM today, and a Red 
Flag Warning is in effect from 2 AM to 6 PM today. Sunday into 
next week, offshore winds will continue but trend weaker each day.
At this point no hazard products for wind or fire weather are 
anticipated beyond today.

The wind pattern will bring warm, dry, and sunny conditions to 
the area. Highs will peak over the weekend, with mid 80s to around
90 degrees common for coasts and valleys. Areas of moderate 
HeatRisk will occur through at least Sunday, focused over the 
beaches and coastal plains. Monday temperatures will cool a couple
degrees, as winds weaken and the airmass aloft cools slightly. 
Temperatures will still remain quite a bit above normal, however,
into next week. Due to the very dry conditions, overnight 
temperatures in wind- sheltered and interior areas will fall into 
the 30s and 40s each night. Conversely, windy locations and areas 
near the coast will see warmer lows, with some foothill and valley
locations remaining in the upper 60s overnight.

.LONG TERM (TUE-FRI)...06/621 PM.

Tuesday through Wednesday temperatures will remain warm, though 
slightly cooler than the peak of the heat forecasted for this 
weekend. Expect around 5 to 10 degrees above normal mid-week, with
widespread highs in the 80s. Weak offshore flow will persist 
through Wednesday, thus marine layers clouds will be minimal and 
most likely non- existent.

Starting Thursday, onshore flow will increase and 500 mb heights 
are favored to plummet as a trough approaches the region. 
Temperatures are expected to fall to near normal by Friday with 
widespread highs in the the 70s. As for rain, ensembles indicate a
potential storm system sometime between next Friday and the 
following Tuesday (Nov 13-17th), or possibly even beyond that. 
There is high uncertainty and details remain very fuzzy to say the
least. Possible outcomes range all the way from minimal rain up 
to a significant storm system with periods of heavy rain. As this 
potential storm is still very far in the future, please keep up to
date with the forecast for the latest updates.

a combination of SCA level winds and seas. For Monday through

and seas remaining below SCA levels.

Point Mugu to Santa Monica, there is a 60-80% chance of SCA level 
northeast winds this morning, and a 30-40% chance on Sunday.

.BEACHES...07/121 AM.

High tides will build each morning and peak Sunday and Monday at
7.2 to 7.6 feet (MLLW). Meanwhile, a west to northwest swell will
slowly build into the area, peaking on Monday. This combination 
of high tides and high surf will bring hazardous swimming 
conditions, dangerous conditions on rock jetties, and a risk for 
moderate coastal flooding. If you are in the coastal areas, listen
to advice from your local officials.

With the daily high tides changing only a little through Tuesday,
the risk for coastal flooding will peak when the surf peaks 
on Monday. This coastal flooding event will differ in several 
ways from the past episodes this year. First, while tides will be 
high, they will not be nearly as high as the record breaking tides
from last week. This means that the impacts to harbor areas and 
Naples Island will generally be minor compared to last week. 
Shallow flooding should be expected, especially for low-lying 
walkways, but of a lesser degree less in severity and coverage. 
Second, for the beach-side coastal areas, the swell is from the 
west to northwest and not from the south, which characterized the 
coastal flooding episodes of September and early October. This 
means that areas hit hard in those events, like Long Beach and 
Malibu, are less at risk with this upcoming event. For west-facing
shores however, the risk is much higher than events in the recent
past. Areas like Oceano and Cayucos on the Central Coast, and 
Ventura on the southern coasts, have elevated risks of moderate 
coastal flooding. Moderate coastal flooding impacts include things
like flooded sandy beach areas, moderate beach erosion, as well 
as shallow flooding of beach parking lots and bike paths. Isolated
damage is unlikely but cannot be ruled out especially considering
the extent of beach erosion we have already seen - which limits 
the natural protective buffer between the ocean and coastal 
infrastructure. 

For the Central Coast, a High Surf Advisory and Coastal Flood
Advisory will be in effect through Monday, since the peak of the
surf is earlier compared to other areas. For all other coasts, a 
Beach Hazards Statement will be in effect through Tuesday, with a 
key note that some areas (especially Ventura County) may need to 
be upgraded to a Coastal Flood and/or High Surf Advisory around 
Monday when the surf peaks.

.SHORT TERM...

Issued at 159 AM EST Sat Nov 7 2026

A rather potent mid level low/trough complex will push through a 
good portion of the Eastern Seaboard today into tonight before 
gradually pushing off into the western Atlantic on Sunday. While the 
trough axis will remain well to the north of the region, it will 
suppress the mid level ridging to the southeast which will result in 
mostly zonal flow over South Florida this afternoon and through the 
rest of the weekend. At the surface, a very weak frontal boundary 
currently over Central Florida will continue to slowly push 
southeastward through the region this afternoon before stalling 
over the southern portion of the area or over the Keys heading 
into the second half of the weekend. 

Out ahead of the front, some lower level moisture will gradually 
pool over the region as PWAT values gradually increase and will 
generally range between 1.3 and 1.6 inches this afternoon through 
Sunday. Most of this moisture will be in the lower levels of the 
atmospheric column as the latest forecast model soundings show a 
pretty good swath of drier air remaining in place across the mid 
levels during this time frame. The weakening frontal boundary moving 
into the region combined with an increase in lower level moisture 
could be enough to spark off some scattered shower activity this 
afternoon out ahead of the front. With a good amount of drier air in 
place across the mid levels, thunderstorm chances will remain very 
low as the front pushes into the region and continues to weaken. 
However, an isolated thunderstorm cannot be entirely ruled out over 
the southern areas and the Atlantic waters where instability may be 
slightly higher. 

As the front loses its forward momentum and gradually stalls out 
on Sunday, there will still be enough lower level moisture to 
keep just a slight chance of showers in place mainly over the east
coast as well as the Atlantic waters. However, most of the region
will remain dry through a good portion of the day. High 
temperatures for today will generally remain in the lower to mid 
80s along and north of Alligator Alley as well as the east coast 
metro areas. High temperatures could rise into the upper 80s 
across interior portions south of Alligator Alley. High 
temperatures on Sunday will generally rise into the lower to mid 
80s across most of the region, however, some interior locations 
south of Alligator Alley in Southwest Florida could see upper 80s 
once again on Sunday afternoon.

Early morning objective analysis depicts the central circulation of 
low pressure system cutting off from the northern stream and 
descending into SW Arizona. A jet streak on the western periphery of 
this circulation will ensure additional equatorward propagation over 
the next 48 hours taking the cold core and synoptic ascent well into 
northern Mexico. In its wake, sharp high pressure ridging folded 
towards the Great Basin/central Rockies will promote surface 
pressure rises and subsident, dry air filtering into the forecast 
area. Periods of nocturnal/morning breezy E/NE winds will be common 
over portions of the area in this typical cold season pattern, 
however wind speeds should not be very strong or seasonally 
anomalous. Under the building ridge through the weekend, H5 heights 
will rise into a 580-584dm range allowing modest warming versus the 
past several days. Numerical guidance spreads are rather narrow 
yielding excellent forecast confidence of high temperatures within a 
few degrees of the daily normals while overnight lows warm several 
degrees above normal.

.LONG TERM /Tuesday through Friday/... 
Hemispheric pattern amplification driven by an unusually early 
season sudden stratospheric warming (SSW) event will be the main 
story for the latter half of next week with large ensemble forecast 
spread persisting. For much of the week, northern stream jet energy 
will settle over southern Canada while weak low amplitude waves in 
the southern stream remain sequestered over northern Mexico. As a 
result, subsident ridging with nearly steady midtropospheric heights 
will define the pattern over the SW Conus yielding high confidence 
of a very tranquil, near persistence forecast carrying on from early 
in the week. By the end of the week, effects from disruption of the 
polar vortex will be manifested in poleward retrogressive ridging 
while deep negative height anomalies descending equatorward over the 
NE Conus and East Pacific. However, the specifics regarding depth, 
positioning, and evolution of features within the greater synoptic 
pattern remain highly uncertain. Recent operational models peel a 
notable shortwave from the east Pacific trough towards the SW 
Conus/northern Mexico late in the week, however this type of 
solution is not consistent among NAEFS and EPS members. Given the 
amplification phase, wide ensemble spread and large run-to-run 
variations are likely the next several days resulting in low

A dry but cool weekend is in store for central Kentucky and northern 
Indiana as surface high pressure builds in over the region. With
mostly clear skies and calmer north-northwesterly winds, 
temperatures will bottom out in the low to mid 30s by Saturday 
morning. A Frost Advisory remains in effect until 9 AM EST, with

shortly after sunrise. There is the potential for patchy fog to 
develop over the next few hours, primarily in river valleys 
across the western portions of the area. After the dissipation 
of any fog that does develop, it will be a mostly clear Saturday
across the region, save for some upper-level clouds that may 
form in the afternoon. With nnorth-northwestely flow prevailing,
afternoon highs on Saturday will be 5-10 degrees below normal 
for this time of year, with temperatures in the low to mid 50s 
forecast. 

For Saturday night, clearing skies and calm winds will allow for 
decent radiational cooling to take place. The latest NBM has a 55-
70% chance for temperatures below freezing for rural areas, 
decreasing to 40-55% for urban locations. An area-wide Freeze 
Warning was recently issued and will be in effect from 12 AM EST 
Sunday - 10 AM EST. Overnight temperatures are currently forecast to 
be in the upper 20s/low 30s, with the coldest conditions expected 
for sheltered rural areas. To close out the weekend, winds will 
shift to the southwest during the first half of Sunday before a weak 
cold front moves through and switches the surface flow back to the 
northwest. Temperatures will be slightly warmer than Saturday, with 
highs in the mid to upper 50s expected.

Looking ahead to next week, the stretch of dry weather will continue 
as the area of surface high pressure remains overhead. Temperatures 
will fluctuate some Monday through Wednesday, with highs in the 60s 
forecast. Overnight lows will be be slightly warmer as well, 
hovering around the upper 30s/low 40s range. The upper-level ridge 
over the central and western CONUS that is responsible for the 
northwesterly flow we are currently experiencing will begin to 
break down some as the week progresses. By midweek, long range 
deterministic and ensemble models are showing a brief period of 
zonal flow over the Ohio Valley before another shift in the upper-
level pattern takes shape. The latter portions of next week depict 
an amplified upper-level pattern with ridging over the western CONUS 
and troughing over the east. For us, guidance is having a shortwave 
trough swing over the region, though the exact timing is still 
uncertain. This change in the pattern will allow for the return of 
rain chances Wednesday night-Friday, however antecedent dry air 
currently depicted in guidance would keep our rainfall totals down, 
with the most recent LREF only gives a 15-25% chance for more than 
0.25" of rain. The end of next week could bring a return to cooler 
temperatures with highs in the upper 40s/50s as guidance is 
depicting a colder air mass filling behind the system as it swings 
through.

.WHAT HAS CHANGED...

&&

.KEY MESSAGES...
1) Scattered showers Saturday.

2) Gusty wind on Sunday.

3) Temperatures remain near normal with mostly dry weather through 
early next week.

&&

.DISCUSSION...
KEY MESSAGE 1...
A low pressure center will drop south into the forecast area
through dawn and into the coming day. This will also continue 
to usher colder air into the region with high temperatures 
struggling to get out of the 40s. Northwest flow will allow for
the lake to assist with the precip with enhanced rain showers.
The morning may feature a flake of snow or two in Forest County
with the coldest temperatures there. The stronger gradient will
hold off till Sunday but the advection through the day will
still allow for winds to gust up to 30 knots in some cases. Some
showers have the potential to produce heavier amounts as the
NBM does give a 40% chance of exceeding 0.50". 

KEY MESSAGE 2... 
The pressure gradient will tighten up on Sunday on the periphery of 
developing low pressure off to our east. Low level flow in the 925-
850 mb layer strengthens on the back side of it as well nearing 50 
knots over the ridges. Dependent on inversion height, exact 
direction, and potential mixing, Sunday could be gusty across the 
area and especially in the WV ridges. Probability of advisory 
criteria gusts (>46 mph) reaches up to 70% in Eastern Tucker 
County on Sunday. It may be a case that just the far eastern tip
of the county gets especially gusty as the prevailing flow in 
the lower levels is westerly and thus favors downsloping to the 
east of our area. Will continue to monitor over the next 24-36 
hours. In the lowlands, peak gusts being >30 mph are a decent 
bet with probability ranging from 40-80%.

KEY MESSAGE 3...
The early weekend trough departs on Sunday and surface high 
pressure establishes across the Ohio Valley returning mostly 
dry weather into next week with near normal temperatures. Latest
12 hour ensemble trends have turned a bit more in favor of the 
solution dominated by a subset of GEFS and Euro ensemble 
members in which the surface high is slower to build, and a 
slightly more amplified shortwave trough slides through early on
Monday. This would return some scattered showers to the 
northern part of our area and NBM PoPs have nudged up in this 
direction. Regardless, ensembles converge to better agreement 
that the high does become our dominant influence with dry 
weather on Tuesday. The pattern then becomes very deviant into 
the second half of the week as another trough tries to dig out 
of the Great Lakes and quickly amplify over the eastern half of 
the country. How deep it is and when it arrives remain unknown, 
but one would expect that a more unsettled pattern returns with 
surface low development somewhere downstream. That may be local 
or well off into the Atlantic at this point. Once we get a 
better idea of how deep and how progressive the trough will be, 
we'll be able to start to pin down the potential location and 
track of a surface low.

&&

.AVIATION /12Z SATURDAY THROUGH WEDNESDAY/...
A upper low and affiliated low moisture will continue to linger
across the region today, bringing mostly MVFR cigs (>75%). There
is a chance that FKL/DUJ/BVI may dip into IFR within any rain
showers that may occur, but at this point, this is only 25% to 
50% likely and only noted at prevailing for FKL. 

During peak heating, there also may be a few showers that pop up
at other ports, with most guidance forecasting this to occur
sometime between 16Z and 23Z, it at all. Winds may gust through

Pretty quiet forecast heading through the end of the work week as

centered over Hudson Bay today will send a trough down through the 
Great Lakes on the nose of a mid level jet streak tonight. This 
opens the door for broad troughing to encompass a portion of the 
northern Great Lakes while high pressure slides through the Midwest 
into the Ohio Valley building a stable airmass across the southern 
Great Lakes. For tonight, northwesterly cool flow over the 
relatively warm lakes will provide a boost to instability and though 
moisture is weak, PWATs roughly 0.6 inches, there could be enough 
concentrated moisture in the region of steeper low/mid level lapse 
rates to allow some scattered showers or even a thunderstorm over 
the north half of Lake Huron. Further south into the Thumb, moisture 
is even thinner and forcing weaker, but the cool airmass and low 
level jet could be enough to touch off some scattered showers over 
the Thumb this evening into tonight. Current radar over the U.P. 
does have thunderstorms present adding to the confidence of weak 
storms over northern Huron later. 

High pressure then expands back northward across the region ending 
any rain chances Thursday into Friday. Cool air within the trough 
will drop 850mb temps into the single digits above 0C leading to 
cool highs in the 60s to end the week. Clearing skies under the 
ridge with the cool airmass in place could allow some low temps to 
fall into the upper 30s Thursday night in some of the cooler spots, 
otherwise low 40s could be in store for most locations.

touch 80F in the Saginaw Valley with upper 70s for most other 
locations. The warm front leading the way could touch off a few 
showers after 00Z Saturday with the bubble of stronger theta e 
lifting through the area. Though model output is not strong in 
producing rain, we've see these leading theta e gradients on 
elevated warm fronts produce narrow brief areas of showers many 
times. For now, we'll note it and see if we need to add POPs later.

northward into the Ohio Valley before getting caught in the 
westerlies and forced to the east coast. This brings the rain shield 
into Lower MI Saturday night and/or Sunday. Details will come 
together in the coming days, but for now expect a gradient of rain 
from south to north with the highest totals over southern lower MI. 
Abundant moisture with a tropical system will lead to efficient rain 
production for any areas that get clipped by the rain shield.

front extending from low pressure near James Bay crosses the central 
Great Lakes. The lighter gradient winds also veer west-northwesterly 
behind the front early tonight. However, an uptick in speeds returns 
late tonight or early Wednesday as the upper level jet deepens over 
the region. Stability trends lower with the slightly cooler airmass,

delivers some elevated gusts. Potential exists for gusts to around 
30 knots over portions of Lake Huron Thursday afternoon, with 
marginal gusts to gales possible for northern Huron. A Small Craft

frequency of 25+ knot gusts, but any higher end gusts further north 
should be infrequent enough to preclude a Gale Warning. Mid/Upper 
Mississippi Valley high pressure then expands into the area Thursday 
night and Friday offering weaker winds with a southerly shift.

combined with mostly clear skies could support additional fog 
development Sunday night into Monday morning.

Surface analysis shows high pressure centered over eastern Kansas 
and western Missouri early this morning with well-defined clearing 
in the stratus deck extending through central/southeast Missouri in 
the latest GOES-19 microphysics satellite imagery. Raw metar plots

aggressive in picking out lower dewpoint values and drying trends, 
suggesting dewpoints fall another 2-3 degrees, favoring the lower 
quartile of the REFS guidance. Forecast lows in the upper 20s to low-
30s are on track with locally cooler readings in outlying areas, 
especially north of I-70. 

What has also become well-defined is the development of river steam 
fog north of the Mississippi River confluence. Latest USGS data 
reflects Mississippi River temperatures in the mid-50s near Quincy, 
IL to the low-60s near Cape Girardeau. As air continues to cool 
tonight, additional river steam fog is likely to develop at other 
locations paralleling main rivers/tributaries. Early morning 
commuters should remain cautious when approaching bridges, where 
rapid visibility restrictions are likely. 

Today's temperatures won't be far off the mark from yesterday's with 
highs ranging through the 50s. High pressure remains in control 
tonight, though the coolest air shifts south of I-70 as westerly 
flow increases around the northern side of the ridge and high clouds 
accompany the southeast progression of an upper level trough. The 
late night/early morning time of high clouds over the northwestern 
portion of the CWA could be enough to inhibit lows from making it to 
freezing, while upper 20s and low-30s are spread across southeast 
Missouri and southwest Illinois Sunday morning. Mid-level thermal 
profiles indicates 850mb air warms to around 10C, an increase of 
approximately 3-5C. This brings temperatures near normal for Sunday

.LONG TERM /SUNDAY NIGHT THROUGH FRIDAY/...
Issued at 332 AM CST Sat Nov 7 2026

Milder conditions are expected with near to above normal 
temperatures through Wednesday. Seasonably cool temperatures return 
late in the week with dry weather favored through much of the period.

(Monday through Wednesday) 

The northern stream remains active and departed to the north with 
several upper level disturbances traversing the northern CONUS and 
southern Canadian Provinces. Meanwhile, a broad, closed low evolves 
into and open wave as it slowly crosses Texas moves eastward into 
the Gulf States. The axis to a low amplitude mid-level ridge 
approaches the Mississippi Valley Monday, being closely followed by 
a mid-level trough. Both features progressively become more muted 
through Wednesday as mid-level temperatures in the mid-teens (C) 
over the northern Plains are moderated before reaching the 
Mississippi Valley thanks to northwesterly flow aloft. The only hint 
at rain comes late Wednesday as a weak surface low develops near the 
Missouri/Arkansas border and quickly moves eastward. The system is 
not well organized at this stage, lacking both moisture and broad 
support for beneficial rainfall. Highs are expected to be in the 60s 
each afternoon. Chilly morning lows in the 30s/40s Monday give way 
to the 40s Tuesday and Wednesday morning. 

(Thursday through Saturday) 

Both GFS/ECM global guidance show a long wave trough enveloping the 
eastern CONUS through the later portion of the period, though its 
development and exact evolution give rise to increasing spread 
through the later portion of the period. Despite the disagreement, 
the general characteristics are becoming more clear, including 
seasonably cool or chilly temperature late in the week into next 
weekend. LREF ensembles show the greatest spread in the upper level 
pressure pattern extending from the Dakotas through Oklahoma, 
indicating uncertainty in the depth or breadth of its influence. 
ECMWF/GFS Ensembles do agree, in characteristic, that cooler 
conditions arrive by Thursday with the coolest air arriving Friday. 
Spread decrease briefly when surrounding the cooler air before 
expanding once again Saturday, suggesting timing differences in the 
eastward progression of the longwave trough. Several embedded 
shortwaves rotate down the western side of the trough, though the 
number, placement, and timing of these features are not well handled 
at this distance in time, though low end precipitation potential 
may become more evident as we progress through the week.
